paragraphs: Adder neural networks replace multiplication-based computations with additions, offering a route to lower energy consumption. This paper investigates whether their success in image classification can extend to object detection. Detection requires both recognizing objects and locating them, so the study examines how to adapt the network components used for that task.

The authors identify an important training choice: batch normalization statistics in the pretrained adder backbone should continue updating. They connect this requirement to the relatively large variance of AdderNet features. They also add shortcut connections in the detector’s neck and introduce a feature fusion architecture to address sparse features produced by adder layers.

Ablation studies examine the design choices, and comparisons use COCO and PASCAL VOC. The proposed Adder FCOS reaches 37.8% average precision on the COCO validation set, with performance comparable to its convolutional counterpart and about a 1.4-fold energy reduction. These results support the practical potential of addition-based detection when its training and feature-processing architecture are adapted appropriately.
neurips-2021-an-empirical-study-of-adder.tldr: Adapting normalization and feature fusion lets an addition-based object detector achieve comparable accuracy with lower energy consumption.

paragraphs: Distributed training can lose time coordinating workers and exchanging model updates. Decentralized methods remove the need for a central coordinator, but their analyses often still assume global communication rounds. This paper studies asynchronous gossip, where communication happens through randomly selected pairs of nodes rather than synchronized rounds involving the whole system.

The proposed SwarmSGD combines three ways to reduce communication overhead: workers can communicate without blocking, send quantized updates, and take local optimization steps between exchanges. The authors prove convergence with all three mechanisms operating together, even when data distributions differ across nodes and the communication graph is heterogeneous. Their analysis draws a new connection to multidimensional load-balancing processes.

The implementation is evaluated in a supercomputing environment. It can improve end-to-end training time over earlier decentralized methods and, on certain tasks, rival carefully tuned large-batch SGD. The contribution therefore links a convergence result for a relaxed communication setting with evidence that the same flexibility can translate into faster training in practice.
neurips-2021-asynchronous-decentralized-.tldr: SwarmSGD converges with asynchronous pairwise communication, quantized updates, and local steps, while showing practical training-time benefits.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must choose actions using a fixed dataset that may leave many possibilities unexplored. Pessimism helps avoid trusting unsupported predictions, but excessive caution can also hide good policies. This paper changes where pessimism is applied so that caution respects the relationships between values imposed by the learning problem.

Rather than constructing a separate lower bound at every state and action, the method considers value functions consistent with the Bellman equations and applies pessimism at the initial state. Its theoretical guarantees require Bellman closedness, a property of the function class used to represent values. Under that assumption, the authors obtain guarantees where bonus-based pessimism does not provide them.

For linear function approximation with stronger expressivity assumptions and a finite action space, the sample-complexity result improves on a recent bonus-based approach by an O(d) factor. The algorithms also adapt automatically to the best bias–variance tradeoff in hindsight. This matters because it reduces reliance on choosing additional tradeoff hyperparameters before learning.
neurips-2021-bellman-consistent-pessimis.tldr: Applying pessimism over Bellman-consistent value functions gives offline reinforcement learning stronger guarantees without excessive pointwise caution.

paragraphs: A useful reasoning strategy should sometimes handle harder problems simply by spending more time on them. Ordinary feed-forward networks have a sequential computation budget tied to their depth, which makes this kind of extension difficult. The paper asks whether a recurrent network can learn a reusable procedure from easy examples and run it longer on harder ones.

The networks are trained on simple problem instances using relatively few recurrent steps. At inference time, they receive additional recurrences, allowing the same learned computation to be applied repeatedly. The central experiment is therefore whether extra execution time can extend a learned reasoning process beyond the difficulty encountered during training.

The authors demonstrate this behavior for prefix sums, mazes, and chess. In all three domains, networks trained on simpler instances solve substantially more complex problems by performing more recurrent computation. The findings provide evidence of algorithm-like generalization in these settings: learning can produce a process whose useful reasoning depth increases at test time.
neurips-2021-can-you-learn-an-algorithm-.tldr: Recurrent networks trained on easy problems can solve harder instances by running their learned computation for more steps.

paragraphs: An online learner continually updates its model as data arrives, but earlier observations may become less relevant when the data distribution changes. This paper addresses shifts whose frequency and strength are unknown. It develops a Bayesian approach that jointly infers whether a change has occurred and adapts the model to the new conditions.

A binary change variable controls an informative prior. When the method detects a change, tempering partially removes the influence of previous model updates, making room for new evidence. Beam search maintains several possible histories of change points, and the method selects the most probable history in hindsight. This allows uncertainty about when changes happened to remain part of inference.

The approach combines ideas from change-point detection, switching dynamical systems, and Bayesian online learning. It is model-agnostic and applies to supervised or unsupervised learning, including concept drift and covariate drift. The reported improvements over existing Bayesian online approaches support the value of connecting change detection directly to selective forgetting and subsequent adaptation.
neurips-2021-detecting-and-adapting-to-i.tldr: A Bayesian online learner detects irregular distribution shifts and selectively weakens past information to adapt.

paragraphs: Models that combine discrete choices with continuous neural computations can offer compositional structure and better interpretability. A common training approach uses stochastic softmax tricks to integrate discrete distributions into neural networks. This paper investigates what happens when several discrete components occur sequentially along a computation path, extending beyond the simpler structures emphasized in earlier work.

The analysis identifies small gradients and local minima as major obstacles to optimizing these deeper combinations of discrete and continuous operations. The authors propose two remedies: increasing the scale of Gumbel noise perturbations during training, and adding dropout residual connections designed specifically for stochastic discrete-continuous computation graphs. Both changes target the difficulty of learning through multiple discrete stages.

Experiments show that these strategies train complex models that standard stochastic softmax methods cannot successfully train in the studied settings. The resulting discrete-stochastic models also generalize better than continuous counterparts on several benchmarks. The findings suggest that optimization design is crucial to realizing the potential of richer discrete-continuous architectures.
neurips-2021-efficient-learning-of-discr.tldr: Stronger Gumbel perturbations and tailored residual connections make complex discrete-continuous networks easier to train.

paragraphs: Image restoration often depends on a parameter describing the problem, such as enlargement scale, noise level, or JPEG quality. Training a separate network for every setting duplicates computation, while using one network that ignores the parameter can sacrifice performance. This paper proposes a single model that explicitly changes its computations with the restoration parameter.

The functional neural network, or FuncNet, replaces its smallest scalar building blocks with functions of that parameter. Instead of treating parameter settings as disconnected tasks, the network incorporates their relationship into its own representation. This makes parameter dependence part of the model’s structure and provides a way to serve multiple restoration settings through one network.

The authors apply FuncNet to super-resolution, denoising, and JPEG deblocking. They report improvements over state-of-the-art approaches on all three tasks. The findings support the idea that a shared restoration model can benefit from expressing how its internal quantities should vary with the problem parameter, addressing both efficiency and restoration quality.
neurips-2021-functional-neural-networks-.tldr: FuncNet makes network components functions of the restoration parameter, allowing one model to handle multiple image-restoration settings.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks have become effective predictors of molecular interactions, yet ordinary graph networks have known limits in distinguishing some structures. This paper addresses the resulting gap between practical success and theoretical expressiveness. It asks which architectural ingredients allow molecular predictions to represent the geometric relationships and symmetries required by the task.

The authors show that directed edge embeddings combined with two-hop message passing give universal approximation for predictions that are translation-invariant and permutation- and rotation-equivariant. In plain terms, the represented predictions can respect moving a molecule, reordering its atoms, and rotating it. These insights, together with further structural improvements, lead to the geometric message passing network GemNet.

Ablation studies examine the benefits of the proposed changes. GemNet reports improvements over previous models of 34%, 41%, and 20% on COLL, MD17, and OC20, respectively, with especially strong performance on challenging molecules. The work connects an expressiveness result to an architecture that also demonstrates substantial empirical gains in molecular prediction.
neurips-2021-gemnet-universal-directiona.tldr: GemNet combines a universality result for directional molecular networks with architectural changes that improve molecular prediction.

paragraphs: Quasi-Newton optimization uses approximations to curvature information to guide progress toward a minimum. This paper studies the SR1 and BFGS families and establishes improved explicit local superlinear convergence rates. Superlinear convergence means that the convergence becomes increasingly rapid near the solution, making the precise rate useful for understanding the behavior of these methods.

The first approach chooses an update direction greedily to maximize a specified measure of progress. The authors obtain a superlinear rate that does not depend on the condition number. The second approach samples the direction from a spherically symmetric distribution and achieves the same stated rate, showing that greedy direction selection is not required for this particular improvement.

The analysis connects Hessian approximation with unconstrained quadratic optimization and with general strongly convex, smooth, strongly self-concordant functions. These mathematical settings define the scope of the results. The contribution is a sharper account of local convergence for both deliberate and randomized curvature updates, rather than a claim of unrestricted convergence from every starting point.
neurips-2021-greedy-and-random-quasi-new.tldr: Greedy and randomly selected quasi-Newton updates achieve improved condition-number-free local superlinear convergence rates.

paragraphs: A network’s parameter count can be much larger than the effective complexity of the path followed during training. Earlier work links generalization to the intrinsic dimension of fractal structures in optimization trajectories. This offers a way to understand why large networks can generalize, but estimating that dimension is difficult even in moderately high-dimensional spaces.

The paper connects learning theory to topological data analysis through persistent homology dimension. It shows that generalization error can also be bounded using this quantity, without adding geometrical or statistical assumptions on training dynamics beyond those of the prior approach. The connection provides a mathematically grounded route from a difficult complexity measure to a more computationally accessible one.

Using theoretical results and topological tools, the authors develop an efficient estimator suitable for modern neural networks, along with visualizations. Experiments show that the estimated intrinsic dimension can be computed across different settings and is predictive of generalization error. The contribution makes trajectory-based complexity useful as a measurable signal, not merely a theoretical explanation.
neurips-2021-intrinsic-dimension-persist.tldr: Persistent homology provides a practical, theoretically grounded estimate of training-trajectory complexity that predicts generalization error.

paragraphs: Matching points across different 3D shapes is difficult because point clouds have no inherent ordering. This paper introduces a canonical point autoencoder that learns dense correspondences between shapes belonging to the same category. Its central idea is to give different shapes a shared reference surface through which their points can be compared.

The encoder maps an unordered point cloud onto a canonical primitive, such as a sphere, and the decoder reconstructs the original shape from that primitive. Placing the shared surface at the autoencoder’s bottleneck encourages an ordered reconstruction. After training, points from different instances are treated as corresponding when they map to the same location on the canonical surface.

The method needs neither annotations nor a separate self-supervised part-segmentation network. It also handles unaligned point clouds within a certain rotation range. Experiments transferring semantic keypoints and part segmentations compare favorably with state-of-the-art correspondence methods. These results support the shared-surface bottleneck as a useful way to learn cross-shape matching without correspondence annotations.
neurips-2021-learning-3d-dense-correspon.tldr: A shared canonical surface lets an autoencoder learn dense correspondences between same-category 3D shapes without annotations.

paragraphs: Particle variational inference represents a Bayesian posterior using an ensemble of models. Its updates include repulsion between models to preserve diversity, but the connection between that repulsion and generalization has been unclear. This paper studies the connection through PAC-Bayesian analysis, seeking a theoretical explanation for why maintaining different models can help.

The authors derive a second-order version of Jensen’s inequality with a repulsion term defined through the loss function. This term makes the inequality tighter than the standard version. They then use it to obtain a generalization-error bound that can be reduced by increasing model diversity, giving repulsion a direct role in the theoretical objective.

The analysis leads to a new particle variational inference method that directly optimizes the derived bound. Numerical experiments show favorable performance relative to existing methods in the evaluated setting. The contribution joins a mathematical refinement with an inference procedure: diversity becomes something connected explicitly to the bound being optimized, rather than only a feature of the update dynamics.
neurips-2021-loss-function-based-second-.tldr: A tighter Jensen inequality links model repulsion to a generalization bound and yields a new particle variational inference method.

paragraphs: Video captioning requires a sentence that is both fluent and relevant to what appears in the video. Many approaches generate one word after another from left to right. This paper instead makes sentence hierarchy explicit, using a graph-structured generation process to represent relationships that a purely sequential output order does not directly expose.

The method first constructs a multimodal dependency tree and then traverses it to produce the sentence. The tree’s topology represents syntactic structure and semantic relationships, while each node contains both visual and textual features. This adapts dependency-tree ideas from understanding language to generating language grounded in images and videos.

Training uses a tree-structured reinforcement learning algorithm with a reward that evaluates semantic consistency between a generated subtree and the ground-truth tree. This supplies feedback about the developing hierarchical structure. Experiments on several video-captioning datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness, supporting explicit sentence structure as a useful component of visually grounded caption generation.
neurips-2021-multi-modal-dependency-tree.tldr: Generating captions through multimodal dependency trees makes sentence structure and visual grounding explicit during generation and training.

paragraphs: Observations and experiments do not automatically determine what would have happened under a different course of events. This paper studies when such counterfactual questions can be answered from an arbitrary combination of observational and experimental distributions. It focuses on nested counterfactuals, which arise naturally in questions about mediation, fairness, and direct or indirect effects.

The authors first establish a counterfactual unnesting theorem. It converts arbitrary nested counterfactuals into unnested ones, providing a way to simplify the form of the query before analyzing whether the available evidence determines it. They then give a graphical condition that is both necessary and sufficient for counterfactual identification from the supplied distributions.

An efficient, complete algorithm turns these results into an identification procedure. If it returns an expression, that expression identifies the requested quantity; if it fails to do so, the query is not identifiable in the stated setting. This completeness distinguishes insufficient information from a mere failure to find a suitable expression.
neurips-2021-nested-counterfactual-ident.tldr: An unnesting theorem and complete algorithm determine when nested counterfactuals are identifiable from combined observational and experimental evidence.

paragraphs: A lender only learns whether an applicant repays after issuing a loan. A model that rejects a creditworthy applicant therefore misses the evidence that could correct its mistake. This feedback loop can trap a classifier in self-confirming decisions and cause regret to accumulate indefinitely. The paper addresses this selective-feedback problem with a method usable by deep neural networks.

Pseudo-Label Optimism, or PLOT, temporarily assigns favorable labels to a subset of the points currently awaiting decisions. It trains on the observations collected so far together with those optimistically labeled points, then uses the resulting model to decide. The intervention makes optimism part of training rather than requiring a direct adjustment to neural-network predictions.

PLOT performs competitively on three challenging benchmarks with minimal hyperparameter tuning. The authors also establish logarithmic regret under a Lipschitz and logistic mean-label model and a separability condition on the data. The empirical results support its practicality, while the conditional guarantee explains when its optimistic exploration can control accumulated decision errors.
neurips-2021-neural-pseudo-label-optimis.tldr: PLOT trains neural classifiers with optimistic temporary labels to counter feedback loops caused by observing outcomes only for accepted decisions.

paragraphs: Two-sample testing asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMD, supplies a statistic for this task, but its computational and memory demands can make repeated updates difficult. This paper introduces a neural-network MMD statistic through a connection with the neural tangent kernel, or NTK.

That connection enables a computation- and memory-efficient way to calculate the statistic and carry out NTK-based two-sample tests. Efficiency matters particularly when new observations arrive over time and must be incorporated into an online procedure. The method therefore connects neural-network computation to a testing framework whose resource requirements are a longstanding practical concern.

The same connection allows existing kernel-MMD theory to describe the new statistic’s false-positive behavior and ability to detect distribution differences. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution combines a more efficient computational approach with a route to understanding its statistical testing properties.
neurips-2021-neural-tangent-kernel-maxim.tldr: Connecting the neural tangent kernel to MMD yields efficient two-sample testing with statistical properties grounded in existing kernel theory.

paragraphs: Incremental few-shot learning asks a model to keep adding categories from only a handful of examples. This creates a difficult combination: new data are scarce and imbalanced, while adapting the model can erase its ability to recognize earlier categories. The paper finds severe forgetting in existing methods and examines how the initial training stage contributes to it.

The authors’ analysis suggests that protection against forgetting should begin when learning the base classes. Their approach seeks flat local minima of the base-training objective, meaning regions where parameter changes have relatively little effect on that objective. Later tasks are learned by fine-tuning within the flat region, aiming to accommodate new categories while preserving earlier knowledge.

Comprehensive experiments report better performance than all prior state-of-the-art methods in the comparison and results close to an approximate upper bound. The findings support preparing the initial model for future adaptation, with the geometry of its base-training solution providing room for subsequent few-shot updates.
neurips-2021-overcoming-catastrophic-for.tldr: Finding flat minima during base training helps a model learn new few-shot categories while retaining previously learned ones.

paragraphs: Simulation supplies many inexpensive interactions, while real-world interaction provides more faithful but costly experience. A common workflow trains a controller in simulation before using it to initialize real-world learning. This paper instead studies how an agent can learn from simulation and the real environment simultaneously, keeping both sources active during training.

The proposed algorithm balances the large volume of simulated samples against the smaller supply of high-fidelity real samples. It maintains a separate replay buffer for every environment the agent interacts with. These buffers preserve each source of experience within a multi-environment learning process and provide the basis for combining their contributions.

The authors develop a theoretical analysis of replay buffers and use it to establish convergence properties for multi-environment interaction. They also demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in a sim-to-real environment. The work supports simultaneous learning as a useful way to combine simulation throughput with real-world fidelity, and gives theoretical treatment to the replay mechanism underlying that combination.
neurips-2021-sim-and-real-better-togethe.tldr: Separate replay buffers let an agent balance simulated and real experience while learning from both environments simultaneously.

paragraphs: Transducer models are useful for speech recognition because they align input and output in order and support streaming. Speech-T adapts this idea to speech synthesis, where the output is a continuous mel-spectrogram. A central difficulty is balancing the prediction of acoustic output with the decision to advance to the next text input.

The Transformer-based model uses a new forward algorithm that separates transition prediction from continuous acoustic prediction when computing the probability lattice. A diagonal constraint helps learn the text–speech alignment. Adjusting the available look-ahead context lets the same approach support either full-sentence synthesis or streaming synthesis.

Speech-T also supports synthesis and recognition together in one network, with advantages including fewer parameters and streaming in both directions. Experiments on LJSpeech show greater robustness than an attention-based autoregressive synthesis model, attributed to monotonic alignment, along with good streaming voice quality and benefits from joint modeling. The results connect a structured alignment mechanism to both reliable synthesis and shared speech processing.
neurips-2021-speech-t-transducer-for-tex.tldr: Speech-T adapts transducers to continuous speech output and supports streaming synthesis and recognition in one network.

paragraphs: In stochastic shortest-path learning, an agent tries to reach a goal while minimizing the expected cost incurred along the way. The paper introduces EB-SSP, a model-based algorithm that modifies estimated transitions and adjusts estimated costs with an exploration bonus. These changes construct an optimistic planning problem whose value-iteration procedure is guaranteed to converge.

The authors prove a minimax regret rate of approximately B-star times the square root of SAK, up to logarithmic factors. Here S and A count states and actions, K counts episodes, and B-star bounds the optimal expected cumulative cost from any state. This matches the lower-bound rate without requiring advance knowledge of B-star or the optimal expected time-to-goal bound, T-star.

The paper also identifies cases where regret depends only logarithmically on T-star. These include positive costs, and general costs when an order-accurate estimate of T-star is available. The nearly horizon-free conclusion is therefore tied to the specified cases, while the main algorithm’s parameter-free minimax guarantee is a separate contribution.
neurips-2021-stochastic-shortest-path-mi.tldr: EB-SSP achieves parameter-free minimax regret for stochastic shortest paths and nearly horizon-free bounds in specified cases.

paragraphs: Standard Transformer attention has quadratic time and memory costs in sequence length, while linear-attention mechanisms reduce serial computation to linear cost. This paper studies the computational flexibility of Performers, a class encompassing many such mechanisms. Its focus is the memory needed to compute gradients, which matters when training or fine-tuning on constrained devices.

The analysis shows that Performer gradients can be computed without adding approximations while using memory that grows sublinearly with sequence length. At the extreme, the computation uses constant memory and linear time, with input-sequence storage accounted for separately. The tradeoff is increased time complexity in the parallel setting, so memory savings change the available balance between storage and parallel computation.

The approach is fully backward-compatible, making the tradeoff applicable to existing Performer models. The authors identify decentralized fine-tuning on low-memory devices without server computation as a use case. The contribution shows that linear attention offers flexibility in gradient computation beyond its already reduced forward-computation complexity.
neurips-2021-sub-linear-memory-how-to-ma.tldr: Performer gradients can be computed exactly with sublinear or constant working memory by trading away parallel-time efficiency.

paragraphs: Large graphs may be split across local systems, each holding only a small and potentially biased subgraph. Subgraph federated learning aims to train a shared graph model without directly exchanging those graph data. This setting has an additional structural difficulty: connections between separately stored subgraphs may be missing from each system’s local view.

The paper proposes FedSage, which combines GraphSage with federated averaging to learn from node features, links, and task labels distributed across local subgraphs. FedSage+ extends it with a missing-neighbor generator trained alongside the graph model. The generator addresses absent cross-subgraph connections, so the method considers both distributed model training and incomplete neighborhood information.

Experiments use four real-world graph datasets with synthesized federated subgraph partitions. They show effectiveness and efficiency for the proposed methods, while the theoretical analysis provides consistent implications for generalization to the global graph. The evidence supports reconstructing missing neighborhood information as a useful addition to federated graph learning under the studied partitioned-data settings.
neurips-2021-subgraph-federated-learning.tldr: FedSage+ combines federated graph learning with missing-neighbor generation to address incomplete connections across locally stored subgraphs.

paragraphs: Multimodal regression combines several information sources to predict a numerical outcome. Prediction quality alone does not explain how confidently a system should rely on each source, especially when some inputs are corrupted. This paper makes uncertainty estimation part of the integration process, aiming to produce predictions with an explicit account of their reliability.

The proposed MoNIG algorithm uses a mixture of Normal-Inverse Gamma distributions to estimate uncertainty and adaptively combine modalities. It tracks uncertainty for individual modalities and represents both modality-specific and global uncertainty. It also distinguishes epistemic uncertainty, associated with the model’s knowledge, from aleatoric uncertainty, associated with variability in the data.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the method’s effectiveness and robustness to corrupted modalities. Applications include superconductivity temperature prediction, CT-slice relative-location prediction, and multimodal sentiment analysis. These findings support uncertainty-aware fusion as a way to adjust reliance on different sources while exposing uncertainty in the final regression result, rather than evaluating only prediction performance.
neurips-2021-trustworthy-multimodal-regr.tldr: MoNIG estimates modality-specific and global uncertainty to adaptively combine information sources for more reliable regression.

paragraphs: A neural network’s intermediate layers encode visual patterns, but their usefulness for distinguishing inputs can be difficult to inspect. This paper proposes a visualization method centered on that discriminative power. It examines the network from two complementary perspectives: how patterns emerge over training and how patterns are combined as information moves through the layers.

The first perspective tracks regional visual patterns learned within each intermediate layer during training. The second shows how patterns in lower layers that are not themselves discriminative can contribute to discriminative patterns in middle or higher layers. This helps explain how the usefulness of a representation can depend on what later computation builds from it.

The method also counts discriminative visual patterns as knowledge points, providing a way to assess representation capacity. The authors use the visualizations to gain insights into signal-processing behavior associated with adversarial attacks and knowledge distillation. The contribution connects visual inspection with a quantitative description of learned patterns and their role in the network’s processing.
neurips-2021-visualizing-the-emergence-o.tldr: A visualization method tracks how discriminative visual patterns emerge during training and are constructed across network layers.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can require an expanding number of neighboring messages to compute a minibatch. Sampling reduces this burden, but can be awkward for layers using distant or global information and does not accelerate inference. VQ-GNN addresses scaling through compact representations of global node information, targeting convolution-based graph neural networks.

Within each layer, vector quantization learns and updates a small collection of reference vectors representing global node embeddings. These quantized representations combine with a low-rank graph convolution matrix to avoid neighborhood explosion while effectively preserving the messages contributing to a minibatch. The framework includes an approximate message-passing algorithm and a specialized backpropagation rule for learning with this representation.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental support for the sufficiency of the compact low-rank convolution representation. Experiments across multiple graph-network backbones show scalability and competitive performance on large-graph node classification and link prediction. The findings support compressing the representation of message passing as a broadly applicable route to scaling convolution-based graph models.
neurips-2021-vq-gnn-a-universal-framewor.tldr: VQ-GNN scales convolution-based graph networks using quantized node representations and low-rank message passing.
